function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

function.name: write_markdown_tool
function.description: Writes the provided content to a Markdown (.md) file on the disk. This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: write_html_tool
function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below you’ll find two ways to spin up a **Compute Engine** VM (the GCP equivalent of an “EC2” instance) that comes pre‑installed with an **NVIDIA RTX A6000** GPU and runs **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS**.

> ⚠️ **Prerequisites**
> * You must have a Google Cloud project (`PROJECT_ID`) with billing enabled.
> * The **Compute Engine API** must be enabled for that project.
> * Your user/service account must have `roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1` (or higher) and `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser`.
> * The **NVIDIA GPU drivers** are not automatically installed – you’ll need to run the driver install script after the instance boots (see the “Post‑creation steps” section).

---

## 1️⃣ gcloud CLI Command

```bash
gcloud compute instances create rtx-a6000-demo \
    --project=${PROJECT_ID} \
    --zone=us-central1-a \
    --machine-type=n1-standard-8 \          # 8 vCPU / 30 GB RAM
    --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1 \
    --image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size=100GB \
    --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
    --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
    --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM allocation. `n1-standard-8` gives 8 vCPUs & 30 GiB RAM – plenty for a single RTX A6000. |
| `--accelerator` | Adds the GPU. `count=1` means one RTX A6000. |
| `--image-family` + `--image-project` | Pulls the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image from the official Ubuntu Cloud image repository. |
| `--boot-disk-size` / `--boot-disk-type` | SSD boot disk of 100 GB. |
| `--maintenance-policy=MIGRATE` | Allows live migration during maintenance windows. |
| `--scopes` | Grants full Cloud Platform scope so the instance can install drivers via the metadata startup script. |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Optional: points to a shell script that installs NVIDIA drivers automatically at first boot. |

#### Example `startup.sh` (optional)

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Install NVIDIA driver
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y linux-headers-$(uname -r)
wget https://dl.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.8.0-1_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.8.0-1_amd64.deb
sudo apt-key adv --fetch-keys https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/7fa2af80.pub
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y cuda-drivers
# Reboot to load new kernel modules
sudo reboot
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer not to reboot automatically, remove the `sudo reboot` line and manually SSH into the instance once the driver package is installed.

---

## 2️⃣ REST API Call (JSON)

If you’re calling the Compute Engine API directly (e.g., from a custom automation script), here’s a minimal JSON payload you’d POST to:

```
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/us-central1-a/instances
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json
```

### Sample Request Body

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-demo",
  "machineType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/us-central1-a/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/us-central1-a/types/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update\napt-get install -y linux-headers-$(uname -r)\nwget https://dl.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.8.0-1_amd64.deb\ndpkg -i cuda-repo-ubuntu2004_11.8.0-1_amd64.deb\napt-key adv --fetch-keys https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/7fa2af80.pub\napt-get update\napt-get install -y cuda-drivers\nreboot"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
```

> **Notes:**
> * Replace `${PROJECT_ID}` with your actual project ID.
> * The `metadata.startup-script` field contains the same driver‑install script shown above. If you omit it, you’ll need to SSH in later to install drivers manually.
> * The `tags.items` array opens ports 80/443 if you plan to host a web app.

---

## 3️⃣ Post‑Creation Steps

1. **Verify GPU availability**  
   ```bash
   gcloud compute instances describe rtx-a6000-demo --format="get(accelerators)"
   ```
   Should show `nvidia-tesla-a6000`.

2. **Check driver status**  
   After the instance reboots, SSH in:
   ```bash
   ssh ubuntu@<EXTERNAL_IP>
   nvidia-smi
   ```
   You should see the RTX A6000 listed with driver version ≥ 515.x.

3. **Install CUDA Toolkit (if needed)**  
   ```bash
   sudo apt-get install -y cuda-toolkit-11-8
   ```

4. **Optional: Enable GPU monitoring**  
   Add the following to `/etc/systemd/system/gpu-monitor.service`:
   ```ini
   [Unit]
   Description=GPU Monitoring Service
   After=network.target

   [Service]
   ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /home/ubuntu/gpu_monitor.py
   Restart=always

   [Install]
   WantedBy=multi-user.target
   ```
   Then reload systemd and start the service:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
   sudo systemctl enable gpu-monitor
   sudo systemctl start gpu-monitor
   ```

---

## 4️⃣ Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Task | CLI | REST |
|------|-----|------|
| Create instance | `gcloud compute instances create ...` | `POST /instances` |
| List instances | `gcloud compute instances list` | `GET /instances` |
| Delete instance | `gcloud compute instances delete INSTANCE_NAME` | `DELETE /instances/INSTANCE_NAME` |
| Inspect GPU details | `gcloud compute instances describe INSTANCE_NAME --format="get(accelerators)"` | `GET /instances/INSTANCE_NAME` (look under `guestAccelerators`) |
| Attach additional disks | `gcloud compute instances attach-disk ...` | `PATCH /instances/INSTANCE_NAME` (add to `disks` array) |

---

### Final Checklist

- ✅ Project has Compute Engine API enabled.  
- ✅ Billing is active.  
- ✅ You have the necessary IAM roles.  
- ✅ You’ve verified the GPU quota for your region (`nvidia-tesla-a6000`).  

Once those are in place, just copy/paste the gcloud command or the JSON payload into your preferred tool, hit **Create**, and you’ll have a ready‑to‑go Ubuntu 20.04 VM with an RTX A6000 GPU in minutes!
